paper_sections.title: Evidence accumulation detected in BOLD signal using slow perceptual decision making.

description.value: The study tested whether evidence accumulation during perceptual decision making could be detected in BOLD fMRI by slowing decisions with penalties for incorrect responses and separating detection-related boxcar activity from integration-related ramping activity.

spans.text: We assessed whether evidence accumulation could be observed in the BOLD signal during perceptual decision making.
We slowed down the decision making process itself while leaving perceptual information intact.

design.value: Participants performed a slow random dot motion perceptual decision task and a matched control task during fMRI; BOLD activity was modeled with up-ramp and down-ramp regressors and compared between tasks.

spans.text: We conducted an experiment to test whether we could slow down the decision process in this way, and use this to measure the neural correlates of the integration component.

We used a control task in which no evidence accumulation of moving dots could take place, but participants still viewed comparable visual input and gave responses as they did in the experimental condition.

We performed a voxel-wise ANOVA with three factors: task type (dots condition vs. arrows condition), ramp regressor type (up-ramps vs. down-ramps), and participants (modeled as random effects; AFNI’s 3dANOVA3).

We used two criteria to identify areas of the brain involved in evidence accumulation: 1) parameter estimates (beta-weights) must be significantly greater during the perceptual decision making task (“dots” task) than the control task in which participants viewed randomly moving dots and responded to an arrow (“arrows” task); and 2) parameter estimates must be significantly greater for the up-ramp regressor than for the down-ramp regressor, which is indicative of true ramping activity (see Methods).

Participants engaged in a visual decision making task in which they judged the net direction (leftward or rightward) of a cloud of randomly moving dots (Fig. 1A), indicating responses bimanually with a button box.

task_description.value: Participants judged whether coherently moving dots moved leftward or rightward and responded bimanually with a button box; feedback indicated correctness and the running total of points.

spans.text: Each trial began with the onset of moving dots, and participants were free to respond at any time.
After making a decision, participants were given feedback indicating whether they answered correctly or not, and the running total number of points earned.

design_type.value: three ∼20-min runs of four 4.5-min blocks each

spans.text: Both behavioral-only and fMRI sessions consisted of three ∼20-min runs of four 4.5-min blocks each, with a 30-s break between blocks.
The experiment presentation code was written in PsychToolbox (Brainard, 1997).

instructions.value: Participants judged the net direction of the cloud of dots and responded left or right; in the control task they were told to ignore randomly moving dots and respond to the arrow.

spans.text: Participants viewed randomly moving dots (with zero coherence) that they were told to ignore, and were then cued by an arrow to respond left or right.

stimuli.value: A circular aperture of approximately 3 inch diameter viewed from approximately 100 cm, containing white dots moving on a black background; a subset moved coherently left or right and the remainder were random distractors.

spans.text: Stimuli consisted of an aperture of an approximately 3 inch diameter viewed from approximately 100 cm (approximately 4 ° visual angle) in which white dots (2 × 2 pixels) moved on a black background.

task_performance_measures.value: response time, error rate, motion coherence, and points earned

spans.text: We calibrated the motion coherence for each participant individually, so that they performed at approximately 75% and 85% correct for low and high coherence stimuli, respectively.

description.value: Functional images were aligned, slice-time corrected, normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute coordinates, resampled, spatially smoothed, scaled, and modeled with head movement regressors.

spans.text: Functional images were first aligned to correct for head movement during the scan. Slice timing correction was then performed using sine interpolation. Images were subsequently normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute coordinates (the TT_N27 template) and resampled at 3 × 3 x 3 mm3 resolution. A Gaussian smoothing kernel of 4 mm full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) was applied to improve comparison across subjects, and finally, all time series were scaled to have a mean signal value of 100.
We used AFNI (Cox, 1996) to preprocess the fMRI data.

spans.text: Our fMRI analysis used up-ramp and down-ramp regressors, the length of which were determined by the dot motion viewing time for each trial, convolved with the hemodynamic response function.

model_settings.value: ten regressors: up-ramp and down-ramp regressors for dots and arrows trials, plus six standard motion-correction regressors; third-order polynomial baseline detrending on each twenty-minute scanner run

spans.text: In total, our GLM had ten regressors for each participant: the up-ramp for the experimental motion discrimination (“dots”) trials, the up-ramp for the control condition (“arrows”) trials, the down-ramp for dots trials, the down-ramp for arrows trials, and six standard motion-correction regressors.
